entries.title: Europe wildfires: France expands mass evacuations as Spain battles record blaze
entries.summary: Over 20 aircraft have been deployed to fight new fires west of Bordeaux, and Spanish firefighters fear two fires could merge west of Madrid. Scientists say climate change is fueling more extreme fires across Europe.
entries.content:
July 29, 2026

Over 20 aircraft have been deployed to fight new fires west of Bordeaux, and Spanish firefighters fear two fires could merge west of Madrid. Scientists say climate change is fueling more extreme fires across Europe.

As Spain battled its largest wildfire on record and France carried out one of Europe's biggest evacuations since World War II, scientists warned that extreme wildfires are becoming more frequent worldwide.

On Tuesday, French authorities evacuated another 4,000 people from Atlantic coast resorts adding to the 220,000 other people fleeing a blazing wildfire in southwest France.

Fresh fires broke out near the Atlantic resort of Grand Crohot west of Bordeaux, prompting authorities to deploy 23 planes and helicopters to contain the flames.

"The situation remains complicated. We're not out of the woods," said Sophie Brocas, the top government official in the coastal region of Gironde, where Grand Crohot and Bordeaux are located.

The Gironde wildfire has burned an area four times the size of Paris, and resisted the firefighting efforts of a dozen countries.

Evacuees allowed to return in Spain

In Spain, there was a respite for the evacuees as thousands of residents were allowed to return home after firefighters managed to contain major blazes.

However, authorities remained on alert for a fourth summer heatwave with temperatures expected to exceed 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) on Wednesday.

The biggest concern for firefighters in Spain was two large fires that had at times come close to merging into a single blaze in wooded hills to the west of Madrid.

In Avila, to the northwest of Madrid, a pyrocumulonimbus cloud was seen over the blaze. Scientists describe these clouds as fire-generated thunderstorms forming over intense heat sources like wildfires or volcanic eruptions.

"We are feeling a lot of anger and helplessness. It's something inhuman," 48-year-old gardener David Gonzalez said about the destruction caused by the fires in Avila.

Experts fear that incoming heat waves might cause the blazing fires to worsen.

Climate change exacerbating wildfires

Scientists say climate change is fueling hotter, drier summers that are intensifying wildfires across Europe. The warmer temperatures are also extending fire seasons and making these blazes harder to control, straining the resources of European nations.

Currently, the European Union only coordinates the deployment of extra resources pooled from its member states when a ​country requests emergency help. As fires on the continent grow more extreme, however, the bloc called for greater investment in forest management and wildfire prevention.

Brussels is purchasing its own permanent firefighting fleet.

"Climate change ​is accelerating. So, our response must evolve just as quickly," Hadja Lahbib, the EU's Crisis Management Commissioner, told Reuters.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: How Iran, Ukraine wars and El Nino could fuel world hunger
entries.summary: The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East haven't yet crippled global food supplies. Add a powerful weather pattern like El Nino, however, and the risks multiply.
entries.content:
Food SecurityGlobal issues

How two wars and El Nino could fuel world hunger

July 29, 2026

The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East haven't yet crippled global food supplies. Add a powerful weather pattern like El Nino, however, and the risks multiply.

A potentially record-strength El Nino is now intensifying across the Pacific, bringing either drought or flooding to the world's key farming regions.

Earlier this month, the US National Oceanic & Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) predicted a 63% chance that the unusual weather pattern could be "very strong" this year.

JP Morgan, meanwhile, warned last week that El Nino, combined with $100 (€88) oil prices, could spike food inflation by up to 1.5%.

The arrival of El Nino follows two major conflicts, in Ukraine and the Middle East, during which global food supplies have held up remarkably well.

So, could this third crisis bring the perfect storm that tips the balance?

Triple blow to global food security

Russia's war in Ukraine still hangs over one of the world's major grain-exporting regions, where repeated attacks on ports and farmland continue to threaten one of the planet’s key breadbaskets.

The Iran war has driven up energy and fertilizer prices, raising the cost of growing food worldwide and causing temporary supply disruptions for key soil nutrients.

El Nino, which shifts rainfall and temperature patterns worldwide, is expected to be so strong that the World Bank warned recently it could cut rice output by 20% to 50% in affected regions.

Maximo Torero, chief economist of the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), warned of a "compound effect" that could create "a very complex situation" by the end of the year.

"We are very concerned about El Nino and the delay of the monsoon ... in India," Torero told DW.

El Nino is expected to slow down and weaken India’s monsoon season, a vital time for rice planting. June already saw around 40% less rainfall than normal, according to local media.

India produces nearly a third of the world’s rice, the vast majority of which is consumed domestically.

Aside from South Asia, the FAO thinks the El Nino risks are highest in Africa's Sahel region, southern Africa, Southeast Asia and in the Dry Corridor of Central America.

The UN food agency warned this month that some of these regions face a more than 50% chance of drought in the next few months.

World producing more food than ever

Despite the geopolitical strife, food prices remain nearly 20% below their 2022 peak, according to the FAO Food Price Index.

The world brought in the biggest grain harvest in history last year. This is because farmers planted more land, the weather has been favorable and the crops produced more per acre.

While this year is expected to be slightly smaller, the harvest will still be the second-largest ever.

“We are seeing improvements in agricultural productivity," Simone Bunse, senior researcher at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), told DW, citing India and Latin America as notable examples.

"These have helped sustain food production and reduce undernourishment. And this is balancing some of the localized impacts of conflict.”

Millions still go hungry

War is a major barrier to getting hunger under control globally. The UN says 266 million people are still facing acute hunger, more than half of them due to conflict.

The worst of it is concentrated in just a handful of conflict-hit countries, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Sudan and Yemen, where supplies cannot reach the people who need them.

"We have enough calories produced in the world to feed everybody," Torero said. "Those calories are not distributed in the same way across the world and that's the challenge."

War often destroys local food sources, displaces millions of people, damages infrastructure and severely cuts humanitarian access. In some hotspots such as Sudan and Gaza, experts say hunger is increasingly being used as a weapon.

"Parties deliberately destroy farmland, livestock, water systems, food storage facilities, and transport routes. They jeopardize access to markets and obstruct humanitarian assistance," SIPRI's Bunse told DW.

Farmers pinched by elevated fertilizer prices

Another risk to global food supplies is fertilizer, around a third of which normally passes through the Strait of Hormuz. The strait remains heavily disrupted after a failed ceasefire between the US and Iran, along with attacks on shipping in the Red Sea.

Some farmers have been paying substantially more for fertilizer, delaying purchases or switching to crops that require less fertiliser. If they ultimately apply less, yields could suffer in the next harvest.

Food security experts believe the Middle East conflict alone could leave millions more people hungry by 2030 — and that projection does not yet account for the effects of El Nino.

With temperatures in the Pacific Ocean expected to rise by 3.6 degrees Celsius (38.4 degrees Fahrenheit) — almost double the 2015/6 El Nino — climate think tank Berkeley Earth now predicts this year's weather pattern will be strongest on record.

If oil prices leap past $120 a barrel again, if grain exports from Ukraine are successfully blocked, or if El Nino bites harder into next year’s crops as farmers plant less, then the world could face a spike in hunger, experts predict.

If all of those happen at once, the impact would be far worse, with JP Morgan predicting that food inflation will surpass 5% in 2027 and that emerging markets would take the biggest hit.

Additional reporting by Daniel Winter.

Edited by: Rob Mudge

entries.title: The Slovak village questioning its UNESCO status
entries.summary: The picturesque village of Vlkolinec in Slovakia has been on UNESCO's World Heritage List since 1993. Vlkolinec was recently in the headlines for wanting to be taken off the list. DW visited the village to find out why.
entries.content:
July 29, 2026

The picturesque village of Vlkolinec in Slovakia has been on UNESCO's World Heritage List since 1993. Vlkolinec was recently in the headlines for wanting to be taken off the list. DW visited the village to find out why.

From the headlines in the world's media, the story seemed simple: A tiny Slovak village wanted UNESCO to remove it from the World Heritage List because of the pressures of overtourism.

But that's not quite what is happening in Vlkolinec, central Slovakia.

Interviews with residents, local officials and visitors suggest that the debate was less about UNESCO itself than about how to protect a living community from the pressures of tourism.

Accelerated transformation

"Those who come with humility, to admire the village and understand how people lived here, are always welcome," said 68-year-old Anton Sabucha. "They don't bother me. It's the rude ones."

Sitting beneath an awning outside his wooden house, Sabucha leafed through a history of the village, pointing to photographs of neighbors and relatives. His wife brought out a tray of fried dough pastries.

He remembered when around 200 people lived in Vlkolinec. Today, only 17 remain year-round.

UNESCO did not create Vlkolinec's tourism problem. The village was designated a Folk Architecture Heritage Reserve in 1977, during the Communist era.

But Sabucha argued that its inscription on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1993 accelerated the transformation, bringing visitors who too often forget that people still live in the centuries-old wooden houses.

Diminishing privacy

"You come out into your yard, wanting to sit quietly and have a coffee with your friends. Then the first tourist comes and asks, 'How are you? What's it like living here?' Then another. Then another," he told DW.

Sabucha has erected a barrier at the entrance to his property bearing the notices "No Trespassing" and "No Photos." He said that despite this, some visitors still wander into private gardens, trampling flowers and treating the village as an attraction rather than a community.

"Someone sees the 'No Photos' sign and still has to take a picture. They simply don't respect people's privacy."

Disappearance of traditional village life

But the biggest loss, he said, has been the gradual disappearance of traditional village life.

The surrounding meadows are no longer cut, the old agricultural terraces have become overgrown and many of the people whose lives have shaped the landscape are gone.

Tourism income, he argued, has done little to reverse that decline.

Residents receive around €400 ($455) a year from ticket revenues — "barely enough to buy a pallet of briquettes for the winter" — while many of those who now earn a living from tourism no longer live in the village, he said.

"For an ordinary tourist, these are just wooden houses. For us, they're people. We know exactly who lived in each house."

A living village

Justine, a tourist visiting from France, said the village's appeal lay precisely in the fact that people still lived there.

"Usually places like this are museums. Here, people still live here. That's unique," she told DW.

When told that some residents wanted Vlkolinec removed from the UNESCO list because of tourism, she said she understood their frustration.

"Having people walking around your village every day could become unpleasant," she said. "But at the same time, tourism also supports the region. It's difficult to know what's best."

UNESCO status helps preservation

Not everyone agrees that UNESCO is the problem.

Miro Parobek, who oversees tourism for the town of Ruzomberok, which administers Vlkolinec as a municipal district, acknowledged that tourism had brought challenges. But he argued that the answer was better management, not removing the village from the World Heritage List.

"Our first priority is to preserve the traditional architecture," Parobek told DW. "But our goal is also for this to remain a living village. We want to support the people who live here."

He said the town had already responded to residents' concerns by replacing large festivals with smaller cultural events, while residents now met regularly with local officials through a dedicated working group.

The municipality also helped homeowners apply for grants to restore historical buildings and even provided twice-weekly transport into nearby Ruzomberok for older residents.

Parobek said every entrance ticket carried the same message: "Vlkolinec is not an open-air museum. Please respect the privacy of the people who live here."

Balancing tourism, heritage and residents' wishes

He acknowledged that the balance between protecting residents and welcoming visitors was not always easy.

Much of Parobek's optimism rested on plans that had yet to materialize.

Ruzomberok was seeking Norwegian funding for a package of measures aimed at reducing pressure on the village, including a park-and-ride below the hillside settlement, improved footpaths and drainage, the restoration of traditional barns and terraces, and the conversion of the former village school into a community and cultural center.

The project would also create more opportunities for local residents to work as guides and custodians, he said.

Is removal from the list possible?

Anton Sabucha is in a minority. But even if he somehow gets his wish, having Vlkolinec struck off the World Heritage List is an almost impossible task.

UNESCO has removed sites only three times since the program was established in 1978: Germany's Dresden Elbe Valley after the construction of a four-lane bridge, Liverpool's historical waterfront following large-scale redevelopment and Oman's Arabian Oryx Sanctuary after most of the protected reserve was stripped of its status.

In each case, UNESCO acted because the sites had irreversibly lost the qualities for which they had originally been inscribed.

There is no precedent for a community asking to be removed voluntarily.

And there is no sign that Vlkolinec is about to become the first to succeed in its request.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

entries.title: Russia charges Telegram founder Durov with aiding terrorism
entries.summary: Moscow has escalated its pressure on Telegram, accusing the platform of hosting tools used to coordinate deadly attacks and sabotage across Russia.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Russia charges Telegram founder Durov with aiding terrorism

July 29, 2026

Moscow has escalated its pressure on Telegram, accusing the platform of hosting tools used to coordinate deadly attacks and sabotage across Russia.

Russia's Federal Security Service on Wednesday said it had charged Pavel Durov,  the billionaire founder of the Telegram messaging app, with aiding terrorist activities.

The agency also issued an international warrant for his arrest.

The FSB said the charge formed part of "an ongoing criminal investigation" against Durov.

Why is Russia charging Durov?

The security service accused Telegram's management of failing to remove channels, chats and bots allegedly used to organize attacks and acts of sabotage inside Russia.

According to the FSB, Ukrainian intelligence services had used the platform to prepare and coordinate sabotage, terrorist attacks, mass killings and cyberfraud.

These actions, as well as crimes committed by what the FSB described as terrorist and extremist organizations, had allegedly caused numerous deaths, including those of women and children, as well as billions in material damage.

Soon after the news of the warrant broke, Telegram's account on X posted a picture of Durov giving a middle finger to the camera.

What does Russia say about Telegram?

Russia began restricting Telegram's operations in the country last August.

In February, communications regulator Roskomnadzor said Telegram was still failing to comply with Russian law and that restrictions would remain in place until the company met its requirements.

Russian courts have fined Telegram more than 100 million rubles (around $1.26 million, €1.1 million) since the beginning of this year, law enforcement sources told the Interfax news agency.

The penalties were imposed mainly for failing to remove content banned in Russia.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov on Monday said that officials had discussed restoring Telegram's full operations, but claimed the company's representatives had shown little initiative.

Who is Pavel Durov?

The Russian-born billionaire Durov, now based in Dubai, built the Telegram messaging app with his brother Nikolai and launched it in 2013. The platform currently boasts over a billion users.

Durov previously founded VKontakte, Russia's leading social network.

The tech mogul left Russia in 2014 after resisting demands to hand over user data, and is currently based in Dubai.

He describes himself as a libertarian and has repeatedly clashed with governments seeking greater access to the platform.

Durov has promoted Telegram as a defender of privacy and free speech, while critics say weak moderation has allowed propaganda, disinformation and criminal activity to flourish.

entries.title: Germany: How weather extremes impact local agriculture
entries.summary: Heat, drought, heavy rain and late frosts are taking a toll on German farmers. They increasingly respond with adapted varieties, new crops, modern breeding techniques and modified farming methods.
entries.content:
July 29, 2026

Heat, drought, heavy rain and late frosts are taking a toll on German farmers. They increasingly respond with adapted varieties, new crops, modern breeding techniques and modified farming methods.

For many German farmers, the heat wave in late June couldn't have come at a worse time. While barley was already ready for harvest across much of Germany, the drought struck other crops during a particularly vulnerable stage of development.

"This year is another difficult one for farms," Horst Gömann of Germany's North Rhine-Westphalia Chamber of Agriculture told DW.

Corn has been particularly hard hit, as the extreme heat coincided with the flowering period, he said. "We're already seeing some corn plants failing to form cobs. That, of course, essentially amounts to a total crop failure," Gömann said.

In corn, the energy is concentrated in the cobs. If they're missing, yields plummet dramatically.

The heat wave in June, with peak temperatures exceeding 40 degrees Celsius, hit other European growing regions even harder. According to a recent analysis by Coceral, the European association of grain traders, this reduced the value of the grain harvest in Europe by more than €2 billion ($2.3 billion), with France and Hungary suffering the greatest losses.

Due to the heat wave, Coceral lowered its expectations for grain production in the European Union and the United Kingdom by just under 9 million metric tons, a decline of 3%. The London-based research institute Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) even expects a 5% decline. Corn accounts for the largest share of the downward revision in Europe's grain forecast, representing about half of the adjustment.

German farmers need to diversify

The weather also took its toll on wheat and barley. In some cases, barley was harvested several weeks earlier than usual.

According to Gömann, this year's barley harvest is likely to be slightly below average. For wheat, he expects losses of about 10%.

Risk diversification is therefore an important adaptation strategy. Instead of growing just one kind of grain, many farms are relying on different kinds with varying maturity rates.

"You never know when such extreme heat will strike," Gömann said. He explained that farmers who grow multiple varieties spread the risk across different stages of development.

Barley has a natural advantage in this regard. It matures earlier than wheat and often completes grain formation before the major early-summer drought sets in.

Fruit farming struggles with late frost and sunburn

While drought threatens crops in the fields, late frost is a major concern in fruit farming. Due to climate change and mild winter temperatures, flower buds, from which the fruit will eventually develop, form earlier. However, frosty nights can occur well into spring.

Many fruit growers, therefore, protect their blossoms with frost-protection sprinklers. Water is sprayed over the blossoms, forming a layer of ice. "This traps enough heat inside so that temperatures don't drop as low as they would without frost-protection sprinklers," explains Gömann. These systems can also be used for irrigation during long dry spells in summer.

There are also technical solutions for combating heat. Today, hail protection nets serve more than just protection against severe weather, as they also shade the fruit and prevent sunburn.

In addition, experiments are already underway in fruit and wine growing with semi-transparent photovoltaic films. They generate electricity and protect the plants from excessive sunlight while allowing enough light to pass through.

However, while irrigation is an important tool, Gömann believes it is not always economically viable. He said vegetables, potatoes and fruit generate high returns and justify the investment. He added that for grains or corn, irrigation is not worthwhile. "The costs are simply too high," he said.

The water comes primarily from groundwater. Despite frequent periods of drought, Germany is not a water-scarce country. "We basically still have enough water in Germany," the Gömann emphasized. The problem, he said, is rather the uneven distribution. Heavy rainfall occurs in winter, while dry spells are becoming more frequent in summer.

New breeds suitable for a warmer climate

Plant breeding plays a central role. Varieties whose genetic origins lie in warmer regions of Europe are already being cultivated in North Rhine-Westphalia.

"With wheat, for example, we're already making extensive use of genetics from France," said Gömann. The climatic conditions there have, in some respects, already shifted to Germany.

Grains with shorter stalks, known as semi-dwarfs, have been around for many years. Short stalks can bear significantly heavier ears, are less likely to snap during heavy rain, hail, or wind and require less water.

In addition, research is being conducted on wheat varieties with deeper roots. Current research at the German Julius Kühn Institute, the Federal Research Centre for Cultivated Plants, aims to develop wheat whose roots respond dynamically to drought by growing deeper only when water becomes scarce in the topsoil.

Soybeans and millet are only niche products

The agricultural sector is also experimenting with new crops. Soybeans are now being grown in parts of Germany, albeit on a very small scale. Experiments are even being conducted with millet, a crop known from arid regions around the world, also only on a very small scale. Even winegrowing is slowly expanding further north, which is a visible sign of the shifting vegetation zones.

For Gömann, the condition of the soil is at least as important as new crop varieties. He said it is crucial to avoid soil compaction so that roots can penetrate deep into the ground.

Farmers, modern agriculture adapting to climate change

Farmers have always had to adapt to changing conditions, said Gömann. What's new, however, is the pace. While climate change used to take place over generations, now it is noticeable within just a few decades.

"The whole thing is happening quite quickly now," he said.

At the same time, modern agriculture has significantly better options than previous generations. New varieties are developed within a few years, and international breeding companies are continuously working on plants that are more tolerant of drought and heat.

For the agricultural expert, one thing is certain: the increase in extreme weather conditions in the past years is no coincidence. He sees the severe droughts of 2018 and 2019, as well as the recent heat waves, as part of a trend.

"This can certainly be attributed to the emerging climate change," Gömann told DW.

Agriculture must therefore continue to adapt, just as it has done for centuries, he noted, adding that it must do so much faster than before.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: US: Trump's intelligence chief pick Jay Clayton confirmed by Senate
entries.summary: Clayton's appointment comes as Trump lately has renewed false claims about the 2020 election, drawing scrutiny over the administration's handling of intelligence agencies ahead of the midterms.
entries.content:
United States of America

US: Trump's pick Jay Clayton confirmed as intelligence chief

July 29, 2026

Clayton's appointment comes as Trump lately has renewed false claims about the 2020 election, drawing scrutiny over the administration's handling of intelligence agencies ahead of the midterms.

The US Senate on Tuesday confirmed Jay Clayton as Director of National Intelligence at a time when President Donald Trump has started reiterating his false claims about the 2020 election, which he lost.

The 51-47 vote in the Senate was along party lines with Republicans supporting the appointment and Democrats voting against.

After the vote, Trump heaped praise on Clayton posting on Truth Social: "Jay is outstanding in every way, and will do a spectacular job as Director!"

Clayton stresses he isn't 'an election denier'

Clayton will now lead the 18 intelligence agencies, including the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), National Security Agency (NSA), and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), which have been reeling from leadership turmoil and staff cuts.

He is a former Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) chairman and US attorney for the Southern District of New York.

Democrats opposed Clayton's nomination after he repeatedly declined during his confirmation hearing to explicitly state that Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election, saying only that the result had been "certified."

"I'm not an election denier," Clayton said, without directly answering the question.

Trump renews voter fraud claims

Clayton replaces Tulsi Gabbard, who resigned in June, and Trump temporarily installed Bill Pulte as acting intelligence chief.

Pulte, a Trump loyalist with no national security experience, oversaw a tumultuous tenure marked by a roughly 30% staff reduction and the release of 2020 intelligence documents detailing China's capacity to interfere in US politics and vulnerabilities in the election system.

Trump lately has renewed false claims about the 2020 election, drawing scrutiny over the administration's handling of intelligence agencies ahead of the US midterm elections.

California Democratic Senator Adam Schiff told CNN that Clayton's refusal to unequivocally state that Biden won the 2020 election "suggests that if the president [Trump] wants the intelligence agencies to cook up something to justify voter interference in the midterm elections, that Jay Clayton doesn't have the backbone to stand up to him."

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Iran war: US, Saudi Arabia strike Iran-backed Iraqi militias
entries.summary: The US military said it thwarted an "attempted surprise attack" by Iran that came after a days-long lull in fighting. Meanwhile, Israel's Netanyahu hailed an "excellent" meeting with Trump. Follow DW.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran war: US, Saudi Arabia strike Iran-backed Iraqi militias

Published July 29, 2026last updated July 29, 2026

The US military said it thwarted an "attempted surprise attack" by Iran that came after a days-long lull in fighting. Meanwhile, Israel's Netanyahu hailed an "excellent" meeting with Trump. Follow DW.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • US military says Iranian ballistic missiles intercepted
  • The confrontation comes after a days-long lull in fighting
  • US, Saudi Arabia announce striking Iranian-backed militias in Iraq
  • Netanyahu hails his White House meeting with Trump despite tensions

Read below for the latest developments concerning the Iran war and the wider Middle East on Wednesday, July 29, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Reuters: Iran rejects Oman's plan to jointly manage Strait of Hormuz

Reuters: Iran rejects Oman's plan to jointly manage Strait of Hormuz

Tehran has dismissed a regional deal floated by Oman on the Strait of Hormuz, which would see the two countries jointly manage the strategic waterway, according to a source cited by the Reuters news agency.

Talking to Reuters, a senior official accused the US and Saudi Arabia of pushing Oman to advance their "unrealistic plans" for the Strait of Hormuz. While Iran sees Oman as a valuable neighbor, a 50-50 control arrangement would not serve Tehran's interests.

Oman controls the southern side of the Strait of Hormuz at its narrowest point and says it should oversee the waters under its jurisdiction.

The narrow waterway that links the Gulf and Indian Ocean that carried about 20% of global oil suppliesbefore the wartime disruption started in February. It remains a key issue in efforts to end the US-Iran war. 

Skip next section Venezuela protests after Araghchi's remarks

Venezuela protests after Araghchi's remarks

Venezuela has summoned Iran's ambassador in Caracas to protest what it described as "disparaging and inappropriate" remarks about the country's institutions and authorities.

The Foreign Ministry said Ambassador Ali Chegini was handed a formal note of protest on Tuesday. While Venezuelan diplomats did not specify what prompted the move, the complaint appears to relate to recent remarks by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi about negotiations with the United States.

"This is not Venezuela, where they take one person and everyone else gets scared and backs down," Araghchi said, apparently referring to the US capture of former Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro and the subsequent shift in relations between Caracas and Washington.

Venezuela demanded "an end to any reference or comparison that undermines the dignity, sovereignty, institutions or reputation of Venezuela," the ministry said on Telegram.

Relations between Tehran and Caracas have been particularly close since the presidency of the late Hugo Chavez, with both governments united by their opposition to the United States.

Iran was one of the main allies of Nicolas Maduro's government, particularly during Venezuela's fuel shortages in 2020, when Caracas turned to Tehran for petrol.

Maduro is now being held in New York after his capture in Caracas on January 3. Under acting President Delcy Rodriguez, Venezuela and the US have restored diplomatic ties and continued to move closer in recent months.

Skip next section US, Saudi forces hit Iran-aligned targets in Iraq

US, Saudi forces hit Iran-aligned targets in Iraq

The US military says it has carried out precision strikes with Saudi forces against Iran-aligned militants in eastern Iraq.

US and Saudi fighter jets hit several weapons storage and logistics sites, US Central Command, or CENTCOM, said on X.

CENTCOM said the operation followed more than 30 drone attacks over the previous 72 hours. The US military accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of directing the strikes against US troops and Saudi energy infrastructure.

CENTCOM said the attacks on American forces failed.

Earlier, CENTCOM said it had thwarted an attempted Iranian "surprise attack" involving several ballistic missiles fired at US forces in the Middle East.

All the missiles were intercepted, the US military said. While CENTCOM did not identify their intended target, US news outlet Axios reported that they were heading towards a US military base in Jordan.

The attack came despitePresident Donald Trump's announcement that US strikes on Iran had been paused to give negotiations more time.

Skip next section IRGC fires missiles at US bases in Jordan

IRGC fires missiles at US bases in Jordan

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it fired several ballistic missiles toward a US air base and Central Command center in Jordan on Wednesday morning.

It said the attack was in retaliation for US actions against Iranian interests.

"As long as threats against the Islamic Republic continue and the unlawful and hostile actions of US forces against our interests persist, resistance will also continue," the IRGC told Iranian state media.

"Threats by US officials and unlawful interference against our interests must come to an end."

Skip next section Iraq's PMF militia says US, Saudi strike 'killed, injured many'

Iraq's PMF militia says US, Saudi strike 'killed, injured many'

Iraq's Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), an Iran-aligned umbrella of militias, said the US and Saudi Arabia struck its facilities across Iraq on Wednesday.

The PMF said the strike targeted its headquarters in Basra, killing and injuring a number of people it did not specify.

The PMF said the strikes were a "highly dangerous escalation" and violated Iraq's sovereignty.

The US has blamed Iran-backed militias in Iraq for recent strikes on American troops in the region and oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.

Skip next section Saudi Arabia says strikes on Iraqi militants in retaliation for earlier strikes

Saudi Arabia says strikes on Iraqi militants in retaliation for earlier strikes

Saudi Arabia on Wednesday confirmed it took part in US strikes on Iran-backed Iraqi militants, saying they came in response to drone strikes by Iraqi militants that attempted to target oil facilities in Sharqiya and Riyadh.

The Saudi Defense Ministry stressed in a statement on X its "right to self defense."

"The kingdom stresses it does not seek escalation but it will respond to any aggression it faces," the statement read.

Skip next section US, Saudi Arabia strike Iran-backed militants in Iraq

US, Saudi Arabia strike Iran-backed militants in Iraq

The US military said it conducted alongside Saudi Arabia a series of strikes on Iraq in the early hours of Wednesday.

The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) said the strikes targeting Iraqi militias were in retaliation for strikes on US troops in the region and Saudi energy infrastructure by "Iran-aligned terrorists" in Iraq.

"US and Saudi fighter aircraft struck multiple terrorist logistics and weapons sites across eastern Iraq in a strong response to over 30 IRGC-directed aerial drone attacks in the last 72 hours," the US military's Central Command said.

CENTCOM said the latest strikes against Saudi Arabia, which ended a days-long lull in fighting, were directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

"The IRGC and its terrorist proxies must cease these attacks to avoid further US military response," it said.

Skip next section READ: As US-Iran war rages, who's risking the Strait of Hormuz?

READ: As US-Iran war rages, who's risking the Strait of Hormuz?

The Strait of Hormuz has become one of the world's most dangerous waterways since March, when Iran began attacking shipping vessels as a pressure tactic in its ceasefire talks with the United States.

Still, though a significant proportion of the global oil trade bottlenecks at the strait, shipping traffic never completely halted.

With the United States and Iran issuing conflicting statements as to whether the Strait of Hormuz is open, DW analyzed public data sources to track how shipping traffic has changed during the course of the war and which vessels are still taking the risk of transiting the maritime choke point, which connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman. 

Skip next section Netanyahu, Trump cite 'positive and productive' closed-door meeting

Netanyahu, Trump cite 'positive and productive' closed-door meeting

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump and their teams praised cooperation between their two administrations after a closed-door meeting in the Oval Office on Tuesday.

The sit down, the first since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, looked likely to go either way before Netanyahu arrived for Senator Lindsey Graham's funeral, with Trump boisterously complaining about the Israeli leader in public, most notably on Fox News.

Tuesday's talks, which lasted for 90 minutes, were described as "positive and productive" by the White House.

In a social media video posted after the meeting, Netanyahu called it "one of the best conversations I've ever had with the president of the United States," adding that it touched on "our common goal: ensuring that Iran does not obtain nuclear weapons."

Trump said he had a "very good meeting" with Netanyahu in a post on his Truth Social platform.

"Obviously, many important subjects were discussed," Trump wrote, without elaborating.

Tuesday's meeting comes ahead of elections in Israel. The Reuters news agency cited unnamed sources as saying Netanyahu aimed to get Trump's support for his reelection campaign ahead of the October 27 vote.

Skip next section US intercepts Iranian missile attack in Middle East

US intercepts Iranian missile attack in Middle East

The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) said it stopped an Iranian missile attack on Tuesday afternoon.

"Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces launched multiple ballistic missiles from Iran in an attempted surprise attack on US forces based in the Middle East," CENTCOM said on X.

"All Iranian missiles were successfully intercepted. US forces remain vigilant and at a high state of readiness."

CENTCOM did not specify where the missiles were fired.

American troops stationed on bases in the Gulf states as well as Jordan have been targeted by Iranian missile and drone attacks this year.

The latest attack marks an end to a lull in fighting that has stretched for days.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage of the US-Israeli war against Iran.

Conflict has flared up again after the US reported that it intercepted an "surprise" missile attack from Iran against its troops in the Middle East.

Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has hailed "productive" talks with US President Donald Trump during a visit to Washington.

entries.title: Japan: Rescue 'race against time' after deadly earthquake hits Kumamoto
entries.summary: Dozens of people were hospitalized after the earthquake hit southern Japan. According to media reports, at least two women were killed after a shopping mall partially collapsed in the town of Kashima.
entries.content:
Japan

Japan: Rescuers 'race against time' after deadly earthquake

Published July 28, 2026last updated July 29, 2026

Dozens of people were hospitalized after the earthquake hit southern Japan. According to media reports, at least two women were killed after a shopping mall partially collapsed in the town of Kashima.

A powerful 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck Kumamoto Prefecture on Japan's southern island of Kyushu on Tuesday afternoon, triggering emergency warnings and prompting authorities to assess the extent of the damage.

On Wednesday, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said 13 people have been found dead since the earthquake struck. She added that many other people were still missing, suggesting the death toll was not final.

What do we know about the rescue efforts?

By Wednesday, over 9,000 people were in evacuation centers amid the rescue efforts.

"We have received reports of seven people with serious injuries and 29 with minor injuries. Furthermore, as of 7:00 am today (2200 GMT Tuesday), 9,186 people have sought refuge in 506 evacuation centers across five prefectures, including Kumamoto and Fukuoka," government spokesman Minoru Kihara said.

At least two of the victims died in a shopping mall in Kashima and the third died in a building collapse in a town near the epicenter.

Japan's public broadcaster, NHK, reported that "many people" were trapped inside the shopping mall damaged by the earthquake.

Several people were rescued from the mall, including a person who was reported to be in cardiopulmonary arrest.

The collapse of the mall followed an explosion likely triggered by a gas leak, NHK reported.

"Even now, there are people waiting to be rescued, and this is a race against time. We will marshal all available resources on the ground to save and rescue as many people as possible," Takaichi told reporters ‌at her office in ⁠Tokyo ⁠a day after the quake struck.

Authorities assess damage as tsunami threat eases

Prime Minister Takaichi also said initial reports indicated multiple injuries, damage to civilian infrastructure, and fires in several affected areas.

"We are still assessing the extent of injuries and property damage, but I have been informed that there have already been several injuries," Takaichi said.

"Power outages and fires are happening in some areas, and roads and bridges have been damaged and buildings collapsed," she added.

Although the earthquake caused widespread disruption and temporarily raised fears of a tsunami, officials later confirmed that the threat had subsided and that Japan's coastline was no longer in danger.

"This earthquake occurred inland, and no tsunami activity has been observed so far," a spokesperson for the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) said. "For this reason, we hope to lift the tsunami advisory at a relatively early stage, depending on future sea level conditions."

Power and nuclear facilities remain safe

Japan's Nuclear Regulation Authority reported that no abnormalities were detected at three nearby nuclear power plants, providing reassurance in a country still sensitive to nuclear safety concerns following the 2011 Fukushima disaster.

However, the earthquake disrupted electricity supplies across the region. According to Kyushu Electric Power, approximately 45,000 households and facilities in Kumamoto temporarily lost power following the tremor.

Several major industrial facilities are located near the earthquake zone, including operations belonging to Sony and the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the world's largest contract chipmaker. Sony stated that it was evaluating conditions at its facilities, while TSMC did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Japan's long history of major earthquakes

Kumamoto is no stranger to devastating seismic events.

In 2016, the region was struck by two major earthquakes, first a magnitude 6.5 quake and then a magnitude 7.3 tremor two days later. The disaster claimed 273 lives, injured more than 2,800 people. Thousands of buildings were either damaged or destroyed, making it one of Japan's most destructive recent earthquake disasters.

More recently, a magnitude 7.2 earthquake struck northern Japan on June 25, causing little damage and no fatalities. Earlier this year, on April 20, a magnitude 7.7 earthquake in northern Japan injured at least ten people and shook high-rise buildings as far away as Tokyo, prompting authorities to issue a temporary advisory warning of an increased risk of even stronger earthquakes. That advisory was lifted a week later.

One of the world's most earthquake-prone nations

Japan sits along the western edge of the Pacific "Ring of Fire," one of the most active seismic zones on Earth where four major tectonic plates meet.

Home to approximately 125 million people, the country experiences hundreds of earthquakes every year and accounts for roughly 18% of the world's seismic activity.

While most tremors are relatively minor, Japan remains haunted by memories of the catastrophic magnitude 9.0 earthquake and tsunami that struck the country's northeast coast in March 2011. The disaster killed or left missing around 18,500 people and triggered the Fukushima nuclear crisis.

Tuesday's earthquake demonstrated the country's preparedness systems, emergency response capabilities, and monitoring of critical infrastructure.

As authorities continue to assess the impact of the Kumamoto quake, residents are being urged to stay alert for potential aftershocks and follow official safety guidance.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko and Rana Taha

entries.title: Iran war: Netanyahu hails closed-door meeting with Trump
entries.summary: The meeting between the US President and the Israeli Prime Minister is the first since the start of the war in Iran. Meanwhile, Tehran executed two men for their role in anti-government protests.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran war: Netanyahu hails closed-door meeting with Trump

Published July 28, 2026last updated July 29, 2026

The meeting between the US President and the Israeli Prime Minister is the first since the start of the war in Iran. Meanwhile, Tehran executed two men for their role in anti-government protests.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

This blog has now closed. Read below for the latest developments concerning the Iran war and the wider Middle East on Tuesday, July 28:

  • Benjamin Netanyahuarrives in Washington

  • Trump also meets with Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy
  • Iran executes two men in relation to January protests
  • US sets date for next Israel-Lebanontalks

For the latest updates on the war on Wednesday, Jul 29, 2026, you can read our blog here.

Skip next section US intercepts Iranian missile attack in Middle East

US intercepts Iranian missile attack in Middle East

The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) said it stopped an Iranian missile attack on Tuesday afternoon.

"Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces launched multiple ballistic missiles from Iran in an attempted surprise attack on US forces based in the Middle East," CENTCOM said on X.

"All Iranian missiles were successfully intercepted. US forces remain vigilant and at a high state of readiness."

CENTCOM did not specify where the missiles were fired.

American troops stationed on bases in the Gulf states as well as Jordan have been targeted by Iranian missile and drone attacks this year.

The latest attack marks an end to a lull in fighting that has stretched for days.

Skip next section Tehran rejects Oman TSS proposal for Hormuz transit

Tehran rejects Oman TSS proposal for Hormuz transit

Iran on Tuesday rejected an Omani proposal for the equal division of transport routes through the Strait of Hormuz, saying instead that all traffic in both directions must transit through Iranian waters as a matter of national security.

Speaking on Iranian state television, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said the waterway would remain closed if Muscat refused to acquiesce, adding that Tehran had never recognized a southern route along the Omani coast as an alternative shipping lane.

The so-called Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS) — which passes through Omani waters and is recognized by the International Maritime Organization — is currently unnavigable due to the presence of mines.

"This is ​for national security ⁠and not bullying, because when the TSS was for 60 years in ⁠Omani waters, we ​didn't say anything," noted the deputy foreign minister, adding that Tehran would not allow third parties, even those invited by Muscat, to remove mines from the waterway.

The Reuters news agency cited an unnamed Western diplomat as saying Oman meanwhile presented Tehran with a Gulf-backed plan for managing the strategic waterway which involves collecting voluntary fees for passage.

However, a US official reiterated Washington's rejection of any tolls or fees for passage.

Skip next section Houthis claim they fired ballistic missiles at Saudi Red Sea tanker

Houthis claim they fired ballistic missiles at Saudi Red Sea tanker

Yemen's Houthi rebels on Tuesday claimed to have forced a Saudi-flagged oil tanker identified as the NCC Ghazal to turn around in the Red Sea as part of a naval blockade declared by the Iran-backed group.

"The targeting of the Saudi vessel [with ballistic missiles] came after it ignored warnings," a Houthi spokesman said.

Saudi Arabia, which claimed to have shot down drones in another incident targeting oil facilities, did not comment on the Houthi statement.

The pro-Iran Houthis declared last week a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia, threatening to further choke the kingdom amid an existing Iranian blockade of the strategic Strait of Hormuz.

Skip next section Netanyahu, Trump cite 'positive and productive' closed-door meeting

Netanyahu, Trump cite 'positive and productive' closed-door meeting

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump and their teams praised cooperation between their two administrations after a closed-door meeting in the Oval Office on Tuesday. 

The sit down, the first since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, looked likely to go either way before Netanyahu arrived for Senator Lindsey Graham's funeral, with Trump boisterously complaining about the Israeli leader in public, most notably on Fox News.

Tuesday's talks, which lasted for 90 minutes, were described as "positive and productive" by the White House.

In a social media video posted after the meeting, Netanyahu called it "one of the best conversations I've ever had with the president of the United States," adding that it touched on "our common goal: ensuring that Iran does not obtain nuclear weapons."

Tuesday's meeting comes ahead of elections in Israel. The Reuters news agency cited unnamed sources as saying Netanyahu aimed to get Trump's support for his reelection campaign ahead of the October 27 vote.

Skip next section EU rejects Iran 'aggression' against French diplomats

EU rejects Iran 'aggression' against French diplomats

The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in a statement that the bloc condemned an "aggression" this month by Iranian security services against two French diplomats in Tehran.

"The EU unequivocally condemns the aggression against two diplomats of the Embassy of France in Tehran perpetrated by Iranian security forces on July 19," Kallas said.

"Such acts constitute a blatant violation of the Vienna Conventions and jeopardize the very conduct of diplomatic relations," she added. Kallas was referring to the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations.

France said its diplomats were detained in Iran for no particular reason and had suffered "an extremely serious act of intimidation" by Iranian security services, with one of them physically abused.

For its part, Iran's foreign ministry said it had summoned the French ambassador on Monday to protest the conduct of the diplomats.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Who is still transiting the Strait of Hormuz?

IN DEPTH: Who is still transiting the Strait of Hormuz?

The Strait of Hormuz has become one of the world's most dangerous waterways since March, when Iran began attacking shipping vessels as a pressure tactic in its ceasefire talks with the United States.

A significant proportion of the global oil trade has ended up bottlenecked at the strait — but shipping traffic has never completely halted.

Who is still risking the dangerous passage through the Strait of Hormuz — and why?

Read DW's in-depth analysis to find out more.

Skip next section Iran discusses Strait of Hormuz with Oman, Saudi Arabia

Iran discusses Strait of Hormuz with Oman, Saudi Arabia

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi discussed the status of the Strait of Hormuz in separate phone calls with his Omani and Saudi Arabian counterparts on Tuesday.

A statement from the Iranian foreign ministry said Araghchi "emphasized the need to strengthen ​cooperation and advance joint ⁠diplomatic efforts to establish stability in the region, and lift the insecurity imposed ​on the Strait of Hormuz due to the aggressive actions of the United States."

An unnamed Gulf source told the Reuters news agency that Omani foreign minister Badr al-Busaidi had presented a proposal to Araghchi for a joint regional mechanism to manage the key waterway.

The proposal is reportedly based on the model used to regulate the Strait of Malacca between Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore, which uses a system of voluntary fees to fund navigation, environmental ​protection and ‌search and rescue.

The proposal would ensure that Iran would not exercise sole control of the Strait of Hormuz and would therefore be potentially more palatable to the United States and other regional powers.

Skip next section Iran executes two men in relation to January protests

Iran executes two men in relation to January protests

The Iranian judiciary announced on Tuesday that two men convicted of acts of violence during anti-government protests in January had been hanged.

"The death sentences of Abolfazl Sepahi and Amir-Hossein Safari were carried out this morning," the judiciary's Mizan Online portal said.

It said the pair had been found guilty of "attacking police officers with machetes and knives, tying them to road signs, pulling them on the ground, dousing them with gasoline, and setting them on fire."

Other charges, according to Mizan, included "moharebeh [waging war against God] by drawing weapons and creating fear and terror" and "corruption on earth for committing acts that severely disrupted public order and security in the country."

The Mehr news agency reported that the executions took place in "a square in the city of Malekshahr" in the central Isfahan province, in the presence of members of the public.

Two other men were hanged on similar charges in Isfahan province on July 19.

In December 2025, a protest movement initially sparked by the high cost of living in Iran rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on January 8 and 9.

Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, attributing the violence to "terrorist acts" which they claimed were orchestrated by the United States and Israel, while rights groups based abroad maintain that security forces fired on protesters.

According to Amnesty International, Iran conducts the second most judicial executions of any country, after China.

Skip next section Zelenskyy to meet Trump as Ukraine, Iran conflicts overlap

Zelenskyy to meet Trump as Ukraine, Iran conflicts overlap

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is also expected to meet US President Donald Trump in Washington on Tuesday, emphasizing the increasing overlaps between the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine and the US war against Iran.

The meeting comes after Ukraine reportedly carried out long-range strikes against Iranian-linked vessels in the Caspian Sea over the weekend, which Zelenskyy claimed had been carrying military cargo linked to Iran.

Tehran confirmed that one of its ships had exploded in the attack, killing a sailor and injuring several others, with Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei warning that Ukraine's actions amounted to a "dangerous act of adventurism."

The common denominator in both conflicts, according to Kyiv, is Russia, which is separated from northern Iran by only a short sea route bypassing Azerbaijan in the Caspian Sea, or by a 250-kilometer (155-mile) strip of Azeri territory over land.

Earlier this month, Zelenskyy claimed that Moscow has been providing Tehran with satellite imagery of US bases in the Gulf region.

President Trump has played down the impact of any potential Russian assistance for Iran, telling reporters on Air Force One on Monday: "I don’t think they've been doing it, certainly not at a high level. And if they have, it has been very un-impactful."

Other overlapping issues linking the wars in Ukraine and Iran include the stretching of US munitions stockpiles available for each theater and the cutting-edge Ukrainian experience in drone warfare, which Kyiv has been sharing with the US.

Skip next section US support for Iran war in decline — survey

US support for Iran war in decline — survey

Popular support for the United States' war with Iran has fallen to its lowest since the start of the conflict five months ago, according to a new survey conducted by the Reuters news agency and the Ipsos polling institute.

According to the poll, carried out over the weekend and published on Monday, only one third of US citizens remain supportive of their country's military operations.

Meanwhile, 69% are of the opinion that US President Donald Trump has failed to adequately explain the goals of the intervention.

A government spokeswoman told Reuters that the White House doesn't attach any meaning to the poll and that President Trump doesn't make decisions based on fluctuating survey results.

She insisted that the most important objective in the war against Iran remains the degradation of Tehran's ability to produce a nuclear weapon.

18 US service personnel have been killed during operations so far, in addition to thousands of people in Iran and Lebanon, despite Trump promising during his 2024 election campaign to keep the United States out of foreign wars.

The survey put general public support for Trump at 37%.

Skip next section Israel intercepts drone near Jordanian border

Israel intercepts drone near Jordanian border

The Israeli air force said on Tuesday morning that it had intercepted a drone close to the border with Jordan — although it provided no information regarding the potential provenance of the weapon.

According to the air force, the drone did not enter Israeli airspace.

The operation came following the interception of two further drones near the Jordanian border on Monday, the provenance of which also remains unclear.

In addition to Israeland the Israeli-occupied West Bank, Jordan also shares borders with Syria, Iraq and Saudi Arabia, giving it a geographically important position amid several regional conflicts. The United States also maintains a military presence on Jordanian air force bases.

Although Israel took joint part in the initial offensive against Iran back in February, it has not participated in the most recent round of strikes.

Skip next section US confirms next round of Israel-Lebanon talks

US confirms next round of Israel-Lebanon talks

The US State Department confirmed on Monday that the next round of talks between Israel and Lebanon would begin in Rome next week on August 4.

"In Rome, technical groups will focus on advancing the full implementation of the framework agreement," a State Department official told the French AFP news agency.

The Israel-Lebanon framework deal calls for an end to hostilities, the disarmament of militant group Hezbollah, the deployment of Lebanese military troops in the south of the country, and for Israeli forces to gradually withdraw from Lebanon in two so-called "pilot zones."

The official said the agenda would include "resolving all outstanding border issues," among other things.

"The experience of the initial zones will help us perfect pilot-zone implementation so it can expand in a phased manner," the official added.

Despite the framework agreement, Lebanon has reported intermittent Israeli strikes and artillery shelling on the south of the country in recent days.

Skip next section Netanyahu lands in Washington to meet with Trump

Netanyahu lands in Washington to meet with Trump

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu arrived in Washington on Tuesday to meet with US President Donald Trump .

It will be Netanyahu's first visit to the White House since the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, triggering the ongoing war.

"This is a great privilege, but it is also a great responsibility," Netanyahu said before departing Israel on Monday.

"We will discuss all the issues on the agenda, first and foremost Iran. Naturally, our goal is to safeguard our security and also to expand the circle of peace around us," he added.

The trip comes as Trump increasingly expresses frustration toward Netanyahu over hostilities in the Middle East, referring to him in one interview as a "difficult guy."

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage of the US-Israeli war against Iran.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is set to discuss the conflict today with US President Donald Trump in Washington. The two leaders have publicly disagreed throughout the course of the war, with Trump in recent weeks expressing frustration with Netanyahu's actions in the Middle East.

Meanwhile, arrangements are being made for the next round of direct Israeli-Lebanese talks early next month, according to Washington.

entries.title: Zelenskyy visits Trump as Ukraine seeks stronger air defense
entries.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is seeking stronger military cooperation, as Kyiv and Moscow intensify long-range strikes amid stalled peace efforts.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Zelenskyy visits Trump as Ukraine seeks stronger air defense

July 28, 2026

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is seeking stronger military cooperation, as Kyiv and Moscow intensify long-range strikes amid stalled peace efforts.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in the United States for talks with President Donald Trump on Tuesday, saying Kyiv's top priority was securing stronger air defense and strategic cooperation as Russia intensified attacks.

Trump welcomed Zelenskyy to the White House late on Tuesday morning local time, ahead of the funeral for Senator Lindsey Graham, a staunch supporter of Ukraine, who passed away earlier this month.

Images taken from behind the fences at the White House showed Zelenskyy exiting a car ready to enter the building.

White House press ‌secretary Karoline Leavitt described the meeting, which was behind closed doors, as "positive and productive."

Zelenskyy thanked Trump for the "good meeting," hailing the Republican administration's support to Kyiv in its war against Russia.

“The President and I discussed licenses for Patriot interceptor production and several other ideas that could help,” said Zelenskyy on X. “We also spoke about diplomacy — it’s important that the diplomatic process be reinvigorated.”

Later, Trump said on his Truth Social platform that the meeting "went very well!"

"Our number-one priority is anti-ballistic defense and strategic cooperation with America. Peace needs to be brought closer," Zelenskyy had said in a post on X after arriving in the US.

US-Ukraine deal on Patriot production recently announced

The long-strained relations between Trump and Zelenskyy have shown modest signs of improvement in recent weeks.

Since returning to office in January last year, Trump largely stopped direct US arms shipments to Ukraine, instead leavingEuropean allies to buy American weapons and supply them to Kyiv.

However, Washington remains a key ally, providing intelligence and access to the Starlink satellite network used by Ukrainian frontline troops to communicate.

In a sign of improving ties, Trump, in a meeting with Zelenskyy in Turkey earlier this month, pledged to help Ukraine produce Patriot air defense systems, and said Kyiv would be able to produce them "pretty quickly."

This has been a long-running request from Kyiv in order to counter Russian missile attacks.

Kyiv and Moscow ramp up long-range strikes

More than four years have passed since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Amid stalled diplomatic efforts to end the war brokered by the Trump administration, both sides have stepped up long-range strikes.

Russia said on Tuesday that more than 390 Ukrainian drones targeted the Moscow region overnight, damaging residential buildings.

Russian state media also reported that Russian forces struck two vessels, including a ship in the Black Sea that Moscow claimed was transporting military supplies for Ukraine, according to Reuters.
